newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Kim says to review policies on N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Kim says to review policies on N.Korea.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam said on Tuesday his government would review policies towards the North, including provision of economic assistance, in view of the recent infiltration by armed North Korean agents.

"I intend to review all government policies on North Korea, putting emphasis on ways to effectively counter North Korea's strategy for communising the South by force," Kim said in a speech marking South Korea's Armed Forces Day.
"The administration will place top priority on the policy of reevaluating the mobility and efficiency of our armed forces.
"Unless North Korea fundamentally changes its attitude, we will reconsider all assistance to it, including charity."
South Korea had provided rice and other relief goods since last summer, when the North was struck by torrential rains that ruined a large part of its crops.
The two countries technically remain at war since their 1950-53 conflict ended with an armistice agreement.

Under an unprecedented agreement in June last year, South Korea supplied 150,000 tonnes of rice to the Stalinist North in a bid to lessen a chronic food shortage and to ease tensions between the two sides.

Earlier this year, the Seoul government shipped $1 million worth of powdered milk to ease child malnutrition in the North. It also donated $2 million to the U.N. World Food Programme to buy grain powder for North Koreans after a U.N. appeal for $43.6 million in flood-relief aid.
North Korea was hit by devastating floods again this year.

Tensions between the two Koreas have run high since an estimated 26 North Koreans landed on an east coast beach on September 18 from a grounded submarine. So far, 22 intruders have been shot dead and one captured alive. Five South Korean troops were killed during the massive manhunt.
Seoul branded the North Korean intrusion a commando-style infiltration in preparation for wider military action and said it breached the terms of the armistice treaty.

In another speech earlier on Tuesday, Kim called the infiltration "an anti-national provocation to the peaceful unification of the fatherland that should be punished in the name of the peace-loving people of the world".
"Our armed forces must be fostered into crack units of strength capable of smashing any adventurism of the North, based on a firm superiority in power," Kim said.

Meanwhile, North Korea has called a meeting with the U.N. Command in South Korea on Wednesday. Its submarine intrusion into South Korea last month is likely to be on the agenda, Jim Coles, spokesman for the U.N. body, said on Tuesday.
The U.S.-led U.N. Command monitors the armistice agreement.
Coles said Pyongyang had not specifically said it wanted to discuss the submarine incident during the meeting at the border village of Panmunjom.
"But it's not unreasonable to expect that they'll raise the issue. Our position is that we're going to go to listen to what they have to say," Coles said.

Pyongyang has said the vessel was on a training mission and drifted into Southern waters after developing engine trouble. It has demanded the immediate return of the submarine and its surviving and dead crew. Seoul has refused to accept the North's explanation and request.
North Korea has twice rejected protest letters from the U.N. Command over the incident.
"The North Koreans have already demanded that the bodies and the submarine be returned, so we can presume that they may want to discuss the issue," Coles said.
The meeting was requested on Monday by the Korean People's Army. "There is nothing special about it, we have meetings like this all the time," Coles added.
